title: Trump Approval Craters to 36-38% — 74% of Americans Say Iran War Not Worth the Cost
description_short: Trump Approval Craters to 36-38% — 74% of Americans Say Iran War Not Worth the Cost
description_medium: Several polls measured different aspects of Trump’s standing during the Iran war. Economist/YouGov and New York Times measures put his approval in the high 30s; a separate poll asked whether the war was worth its cost. Because the surveys used different questions and field dates, their results should be reported separately.
description_long: Public-opinion measures during the Iran war showed disapproval of both Trump’s performance and the military campaign, but the numbers came from separate polls. The Economist/YouGov tracker put Trump’s approval at 36%, with 59% disapproving, while a New York Times polling average stood at 38%. A CNN/SSRS poll asked whether the war was worth its financial and human cost; 74% of respondents, including 43% of Republicans, said it was not. Quinnipiac separately found that 60% opposed military action against Iran. These results should not be combined into a single survey because the pollsters asked different questions and conducted their surveys at different times. The figures offer a snapshot of public opinion as the conflict continued, rather than a prediction of how support would change. Other measures, including views on inflation and gasoline prices, reflected additional concerns that were not identical to respondents’ judgments about the war.

The flights were part of removals under the Alien Enemies Act. The administration argued that Boasberg’s order was invalid and denied violating a binding directive. Boasberg later found that officials had acted in bad faith and began contempt proceedings. title: DOJ Reversal Allows Seizure of Journalists' Phone Records and Testimony
description_short: DOJ Reversal Allows Seizure of Journalists' Phone Records and Testimony
description_medium: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued an internal memo rescinding Biden-era protections that had barred prosecutors from seizing reporters' phone records, emails, and compelling journalist testimony in leak investigations. The new policy explicitly allows subpoenas, court orders, and search warrants targeting news media. The memo indicated investigations could be launched not just for classified leaks but for disclosures that 'undermine' Trump administration policies — a far broader standard. Press freedom groups called it a landmark threat to investigative journalism and source protection.
description_long: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a Justice Department memorandum rescinding Biden-era limits on seizing journalists’ records and compelling reporters to testify in leak investigations. The policy allowed prosecutors to seek subpoenas, court orders, or search warrants involving news organizations. It also broadened the circumstances in which the department could pursue information about leaks, including disclosures said to undermine administration policies. Press-freedom organizations warned that access to reporters’ communications could expose confidential sources and discourage people from sharing information with the media. The change reversed protections that had restricted the use of investigative tools against journalists. The memorandum set department policy; it did not mean that records had already been seized in every case or that every journalist was under investigation. The decision revived a long-running debate about how the government can protect classified information while preserving journalists’ ability to report on matters of public interest.

title: Hegseth Confirmed Defense Secretary After Scandal-Plagued Hearings
description_short: Hegseth Confirmed Defense Secretary After Scandal-Plagued Hearings
description_medium: Pete Hegseth, a Fox News host with no military command experience, was confirmed as Secretary of Defense on February 4, 2025, in a historically unusual 50-50 Senate vote requiring VP Vance to break the tie. His hearings revealed allegations of sexual assault, excessive alcohol use, and financial mismanagement at a veterans nonprofit he led. Multiple Republican senators expressed reservations before ultimately voting yes. Hegseth promptly began dismantling diversity programs at the Pentagon. His appointment was widely viewed as prioritizing loyalty to Trump over national security competence.
description_long: The Senate confirmed Pete Hegseth as secretary of defense on January 24, 2025, in a 51–50 vote. Three Republican senators joined Democrats in opposing the nomination, and Vice President JD Vance cast the tie-breaking vote. Hegseth, a former Fox News host and Army National Guard officer, faced questions during confirmation over allegations of sexual misconduct, alcohol use, and financial management at a veterans nonprofit he had led. He denied wrongdoing and Trump continued to support his nomination. Hegseth was sworn in the following day and said he would revive a “warrior ethos” at the Pentagon. The confirmation followed a contentious hearing and an unusually close vote for a defense secretary. The allegations were disputed and were not judicial findings. Hegseth’s confirmation placed a politically prominent nominee in charge of the Defense Department, while the Senate’s divided vote reflected the controversy surrounding his appointment.

title: Trump Withdraws US from World Health Organization
description_short: Trump Withdraws US from World Health Organization
description_medium: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order withdrawing the United States from the World Health Organization. The move cut off US funding, which had constituted roughly 18% of WHO's budget, crippling global disease surveillance programs. Public health officials warned the withdrawal would leave the US blind to emerging pandemic threats. The move damaged US standing in global health governance and left a vacuum China moved to fill. Congress had no role despite having ratified US WHO membership through legislation.
description_long: Trump signed an executive order on January 20, 2025, announcing that the United States would withdraw from the World Health Organization. The order directed the government to pause future funding, recall US personnel working with the organization, and identify alternatives for international health cooperation. The withdrawal did not take effect immediately: the United States completed the process a year later, in January 2026. The World Health Organization said the US owed about $280 million in unpaid contributions when the exit was finalized. The decision ended a 78-year US membership in the global health agency and changed the country’s role in international disease surveillance and coordination. The initial order and the completed withdrawal were separate stages. The withdrawal followed a formal notice period, during which the administration’s funding and participation decisions continued to affect the relationship. The change drew criticism from public-health officials concerned about the loss of US participation in global health work.
notes: Needs context: the existing medium says the order immediately cut off funding and claims immediate program effects; AP reports a 12-month withdrawal process completed in January 2026, with about $280 million still owed.

title: Trump University Fraud 'Playbook' Released by Court Order
description_short: Trump University Fraud 'Playbook' Released by Court Order
description_medium: In June 2016, a federal judge ordered the release of Trump University's internal sales playbook, a detailed manual instructing salespeople to exploit students' financial insecurities, push them to use retirement savings, and upsell from $1,500 seminars to $35,000 'Gold Elite' packages. The playbook included scripts for overcoming objections about affordability and instructions not to let students think overnight before signing. Former instructors testified they were real estate agents with no particular expertise. The release severely damaged Trump's campaign and was used extensively by political opponents throughout the election.
description_long: In June 2016, a federal judge ordered the release of Trump University’s internal sales playbook during litigation over the real-estate training business. The manual described sales techniques for moving students from $1,500 seminars into packages costing as much as $35,000. It instructed sales staff to address concerns about affordability, including by encouraging customers to use retirement savings or increase credit limits. The playbook also urged salespeople to keep prospective students from delaying a purchase overnight. Former instructors testified that they had been real-estate agents rather than experts in the subjects they taught. The documents added detail to claims by former students who said the program misrepresented what it offered. Their release was part of a court process; it was not itself the final judgment in the fraud litigation. The episode exposed the sales methods used to sell expensive courses under the Trump University name and became a prominent issue during the 2016 campaign.
